Getting started with RaCInG

Source: vignettes/RaCiNG.Rmd
RaCiNG.Rmd

Overview

RaCInG reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk RNA-seq data. The package supports two complementary workflows:

  • a kernel-based approach for fast, deterministic direct-communication features ("D"), and
  • a Monte Carlo approach that simulates networks and reports direct communication ("D") and/or the giant strongly connected component ("GSCC").

This vignette shows the recommended workflow and the most important entry points for new users, using both the bundled, ready-made example data and a real bulk RNA-seq counts matrix run through the full preprocessing pipeline.

Installation

Install from GitHub 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package")
library(RaCInG)

Install from a local checkout 

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install(".")
library(RaCInG)

If you want to build the RaCInG input matrices directly from raw counts, install the optional preprocessing dependencies used by prepare_input_files():

install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls"))
# ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor:
BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR"))
# liana and multideconv are GitHub-only:
remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv"))

Workflow at a glance

Goal Function Output
Build input matrices from raw counts prepare_input_files() Named list with L, R, C, LR matrices and labels
Compute direct communication (deterministic) compute_racing_kernel() Kernel arrays + feature matrix
Compute direct communication and/or GSCC by simulation compute_racing_montecarlo() Processed Monte Carlo results
Decompose a direct score into ligand-receptor pairs computeLRContributions() + plotLRContributions() Ranked contributions and a LIANA-style dot plot
Compare clinical groups wilcox_group_test() + top_features_plot() Statistics table and ranked bar plot
Relate features to a continuous score correlate_features_with_score() + correlation_plot() Correlation table and rainfall plot

How prepare_input_files() builds its inputs

Starting from a raw gene-by-sample counts matrix, prepare_input_files() chains together several packages so you never have to run them by hand:

  1. Normalization: counts are converted to TPM with ADImpute::NormalizeTPM().
  2. Deconvolution: cell-type fractions are estimated with multideconv::compute.deconvolution() (by default the multideconv set of methods – Quantiseq, CIBERSORTx, EpiDISH, DeconRNASeq and DWLS – or any method(s) passed via deconv_method; the examples below use Quantiseq only, to run quickly), which also standardizes cell-type names to multideconv’s vocabulary (multideconv::get_cell_type_nomenclature()).
  3. Subgroup analysis: multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis() (multideconv >= 0.2.0) clusters highly correlated deconvolution features of the same cell type (e.g. several methods agreeing on it) into subgroups such as "B.cells_Subgroup.1", discarding mostly-zero and low-variance features along the way. Features that join no subgroup keep their full name (e.g. "Quantiseq_TIL10_B.cells"); these names are used as the RaCInG cell types.
  4. Cell-type expression profiles: for every gene, a non-negative least squares fit of bulk expression against the cell-type fractions of each method-signature combination gives one expression value per gene per cell type; each subgroup’s profile is the median of its members’ profiles.
  5. Ligand-receptor prior knowledge: a curated, OmniPath-backed consensus network is retrieved with liana::get_curated_omni() and restricted to ligand/receptor roles, then decomplexified into single-gene subunits.
  6. Filtering and assembly: ligand-receptor pairs are kept only where both genes reach expr_threshold (default 10 TPM) in the sending and receiving cell types, and the Lmatrix, Rmatrix, Cmatrix, and LRmatrix inputs (see below) are assembled and written to output_folder. Each ligand-receptor pair’s per-patient strength combines the two genes’ bulk log2(TPM + 1) expression with fun_LR (default min, i.e. the weaker partner limits the interaction).

You can skip any of steps 2-5 by supplying your own deconv, cell_expr_profile, or cc_network directly. A user-supplied deconv must have exactly colnames(counts) as row names, in the same order, and should use multideconv’s cell-type nomenclature (a warning lists any names outside it). If your expression data is already linear-scale TPM rather than raw counts, pass already_normalized = TRUE; log-scale data (e.g. log2(TPM + 1)) must be converted back first (2^x - 1), since expr_threshold is compared on the linear scale.

Recommended workflow with a real bulk RNA-seq dataset

The examples below use the raw bulk RNA-seq counts matrix bundled with the multideconv package (raw_counts, from Mariathasan et al. 2018, a urothelial/bladder cancer cohort profiled for anti-PD-L1 response) to exercise the full pipeline end to end, from raw counts to features to statistics. These chunks call out to the network (OmniPath/LIANA) and run real deconvolution, so they are shown but not evaluated when the vignette is built; run them interactively to try the full pipeline yourself.

1. Build input matrices from raw counts 

data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv")
counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts)

input <- prepare_input_files(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = "Results/",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq"
)

str(input, max.level = 1)
input$celltypes

2. Run the kernel method

The kernel method is the fastest way to derive direct communication features (communication_type = "D", the only type it computes) across patients. You can pass counts to let the function compute inputs automatically, or supply previously computed matrices via input_data.

# Option A: from raw counts (runs prepare_input_files internally)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

# Option B: from pre-computed input matrices (skips preprocessing)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])

Features are named "Dir_A_B", with the lower-index (alphabetically first) cell type first; with remove_direction = TRUE (the default) the two directions of each pair are summed into one feature. Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor pathway in any patient (structurally zero for every patient) are dropped automatically, rather than returned as dead all-zero columns – so ncol(kernel_res$features) is usually well below the full combinatorial count of cell-type pairs. Lower zero_threshold (e.g. 0.9) to also drop features that are zero in most patients.

Raw or normalized features?

With norm = FALSE (the default) features are the raw communication strength, which grows with both the abundance of the two cell types and the expression of their ligand-receptor pairs. With norm = TRUE, RaCInG also builds a baseline in which every possible ligand-receptor pair is equally strong and reports the ratio of the two: an enrichment score that does not depend on cell-type abundance and isolates which pairs communicate more (or less) than the network structure alone predicts. In the Monte Carlo method the ratio of two simulated estimates is noisier than the raw value, so budget a larger Ngraphs when you use norm = TRUE there.

3. Run the Monte Carlo method

Use the Monte Carlo workflow when you want simulation-based summaries or uncertainty estimates from repeated graph realizations. The same input_data shortcut is available here. Simulation cost scales with Ncells and Ngraphs; the values below are kept small for a quick illustration.

set.seed(1)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  nPatients = 3,
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

# Or from pre-computed inputs:
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

head(mc_res$output$mean[, 1:5])

mc_res$output holds the per-patient mean (mean) and standard deviation (sd) across the simulated graphs. The raw simulations (<file_name>.out, and <file_name>_norm.out with norm = TRUE) and the processed features (<file_name>.csv, <file_name>_sd.csv) are also written to output_folder; they can be re-read later with Read_Sim_Output() and compute_results_processing().

communication_type can also be "GSCC" (the share of cells, per cell type, in the giant strongly connected component) or both, c("D", "GSCC"). Both are then extracted from the same simulated graphs, instead of re-simulating a fresh set of graphs per type – graph generation, not feature extraction, is the expensive part of a Monte Carlo run:

mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)

# output is now a named list, one entry per requested type
names(mc_res$output)
head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])

Patients are independent of each other, so larger runs can be parallelized across cores with ncores (via parallel/doParallel/foreach, so it works the same way on Windows, macOS, and Linux):

mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 500,
  Ngraphs = 100,
  Ndegree = 20,
  ncores = 4,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)

4. Compare clinical groups

Once features are available in a patient-by-feature matrix, use the built-in Wilcoxon workflow to compare groups. wilcox_group_test() reports, per feature and per pair of groups, the Wilcoxon statistic, fold change, and (jointly) FDR-adjusted p-value; top_features_plot() shows the top up/down features by log2(fold change) as a ranked bar chart.

# One label per patient (row of the feature matrix); replace this placeholder
# with your own clinical annotation, e.g. response to therapy.
grouping <- rep(c("Responder", "Non-responder"), length.out = nrow(kernel_res$features))
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 15)

With more than two groups, every pairwise comparison is run automatically; subset wilcox_results by Comparison (or pass a two-group subset to top_features_plot()) to inspect one pair at a time.

5. Correlate features with a continuous score

If you have a continuous per-patient score (e.g. an immune response or survival score), correlate_features_with_score() reports the Spearman correlation between every feature and the score, pooled across all patients and, optionally, within groups. correlation_plot() shows the top positive and negative correlations.

response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)

Understanding the input files

RaCInG requires four matrices and associated label vectors that describe the cell-cell communication landscape for a cohort of patients. The table below summarises each component:

Component Dimensions Description
Lmatrix cell types × ligands Binary compatibility matrix: 1 if that ligand is expressed above expr_threshold in that cell type, 0 otherwise. Rows are cell types; columns are ligands.
Rmatrix cell types × receptors Binary compatibility matrix: 1 if that receptor is expressed above expr_threshold in that cell type, 0 otherwise. Same row order as Lmatrix.
Cmatrix patients × cell types Cell-type fraction for each patient. Each row sums to 1.
LRmatrix ligands × receptors × patients 3-D tensor of ligand–receptor interaction weights. Each patient slice is normalised to sum to 1.
celltypes character vector Alphabetically sorted cell-type names (shared across L, R, and C).
ligands character vector Ligand names matching the columns of Lmatrix and the first axis of LRmatrix.
receptors character vector Receptor names matching the columns of Rmatrix and the second axis of LRmatrix.
Sign_matrix ligands × receptors Placeholder for stimulatory (+1) / inhibitory (−1) interaction signs; all zeros (unknown) by default. Not used by the current kernel or Monte Carlo features.

These inputs are typically generated by prepare_input_files() from a raw counts matrix, or they can be assembled manually from pre-existing deconvolution and prior-network data. The bundled skcm_example dataset provides a ready-made example of this structure.

Running with the bundled example data

The skcm_example list shown above can be passed directly to the kernel or Monte Carlo workflows via the input_data parameter, and to the statistical analysis functions once features have been computed.

Kernel method on the example data 

kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)
#> Using pre-computed input matrices; skipping input generation.
#> Computing kernel for 10 patients
#> Calculating kernel...
#> Calculating features...

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
#>             Dir_B_B Dir_B_CAF Dir_B_CD8+ T   Dir_B_DC Dir_B_Endo

#> Patient_2 0.7127917 0.5965352    1.0316271 0.84989477  0.6860757

Decomposing a score into ligand-receptor pairs

compute_kernel() sums over every ligand-receptor pair to produce one score per cell-type pair, so that score alone can’t tell you which ligand-receptor pairs drove it. computeLRContributions() recovers that breakdown for one sender-receiver pair (exploiting that the kernel formula is linear in LRmatrix, so each pair’s contribution can be computed directly and sums back exactly to the original score), and plotLRContributions() shows the top contributors as a LIANA-style dot plot (dot size = share of that pair’s total score, color = raw contribution).

lr_contrib <- computeLRContributions(
  Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix,
  Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix,
  celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T"
)
head(lr_contrib)
#>     Patient             Edge Sender Receiver Ligand Receptor Contribution
#> 1 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T  TGFB1   TGFBR3 0.0010444341
#> 2 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T  HLA.E    KLRK1 0.0005353052
#> 3 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T    ADM    VIPR1 0.0002670687
#> 4 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T  HLA.F     CD8A 0.0001695168
#> 5 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T  HLA.A     CD8A 0.0001652873
#> 6 Patient_1 Tumor <-> CD8+ T  Tumor   CD8+ T  HLA.C     CD8A 0.0001652873
#>   PctOfTotal
#> 1  21.519765
#> 2  11.029554
#> 3   5.502746
#> 4   3.492763
#> 5   3.405619
#> 6   3.405619
plotLRContributions(lr_contrib, top_n = 10)

Statistical analysis on the example data

The example data has no clinical annotation, so for illustration patients are split by their CD8+ T-cell infiltration (above vs below the median). In your own data, use a real clinical variable such as response to therapy. (With only 10 patients many values are tied, so wilcox.test() warns that it cannot compute exact p-values; those warnings are hidden here.)

cd8 <- skcm_example$Cmatrix[, "CD8+ T"]
grouping <- ifelse(cd8 > median(cd8), "CD8_high", "CD8_low")
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
#>            Comparison           Feature Wilcox_statistic Fold_change    Log2FC
#> 1 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low      Dir_B_CD8+ T               25    3.644724 1.8658095
#> 2 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low           Dir_B_M               25    1.624455 0.6999561
#> 3 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low        Dir_B_Treg               25    1.853754 0.8904495
#> 4 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low    Dir_CAF_CD8+ T               25    1.998395 0.9988417
#> 5 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low Dir_CD8+ T_CD8+ T               25    4.820017 2.2690382
#> 6 CD8_high_vs_CD8_low     Dir_CD8+ T_DC               25    3.317927 1.7302821
#>       P_value Adjusted_P_value
#> 1 0.007936508       0.03968254
#> 2 0.007936508       0.03968254
#> 3 0.007936508       0.03968254
#> 4 0.007936508       0.03968254
#> 5 0.007936508       0.03968254
#> 6 0.007936508       0.03968254
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 10)

For a continuous score, a random placeholder is used below; replace it with a per-patient score of your own (e.g. an immune-response signature).

set.seed(1)
response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
#>   Group      Feature        Rho   P_value Adjusted_P_value
#> 1   All    Dir_B_CAF -0.3212121 0.3676840        0.8720362
#> 2   All Dir_B_CD8+ T -0.4424242 0.2042006        0.8720362
#> 3   All   Dir_B_Endo -0.2969697 0.4069502        0.8720362
#> 4   All      Dir_B_M -0.4060606 0.2473708        0.8720362
#> 5   All     Dir_B_NK -0.5151515 0.1328231        0.8720362
#> 6   All  Dir_B_Tumor -0.3333333 0.3488462        0.8720362
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)

Monte Carlo method on the example data

The settings below are deliberately tiny so the example runs in seconds; real analyses use thousands of cells (Ncells) and around 100 graphs (Ngraphs) per patient.

set.seed(42)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name     = "skcm_example",
  nPatients     = 2,
  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
  Ncells  = 100,
  Ngraphs = 5,
  Ndegree = 3
)
#> Using pre-computed input matrices; skipping input generation.
#> Running Monte Carlo simulation for 2 patients
#> Processing interaction distribution and generating CSV output...

# Direct communication: mean and standard deviation across the simulated graphs
head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
#>           Dir_B_B Dir_B_CAF Dir_B_CD8+ T Dir_B_DC Dir_B_Endo
#> Patient_1       0       0.6          0.0      0.0        0.2
#> Patient_2       0       0.2          1.4      1.2        0.0
head(mc_res$output$D$sd[, 1:5])
#>           Dir_B_B Dir_B_CAF Dir_B_CD8+ T Dir_B_DC Dir_B_Endo
#> Patient_1       0 1.0000000     0.000000 0.000000  0.4472136
#> Patient_2       0 0.4472136     1.224745 1.224745  0.0000000

# Fraction of all cells that belong to the GSCC, per cell type
mc_res$output$GSCC$mean
#>           GSCC_B GSCC_CAF GSCC_CD8+ T GSCC_DC GSCC_Endo GSCC_M GSCC_NK
#> Patient_1  0.002    0.014       0.000   0.004     0.008  0.010   0.000
#> Patient_2  0.012    0.014       0.068   0.070     0.002  0.088   0.002
#>           GSCC_Treg GSCC_Tumor
#> Patient_1     0.012      0.578
#> Patient_2     0.014      0.374

Notes

  • compute_racing_kernel() and compute_racing_montecarlo() are the main entry points.
  • The kernel method computes direct communication only; GSCC is available with the Monte Carlo method. Wedges and triangles are no longer part of RaCInG.
  • Both accept an input_data argument with pre-computed matrices (as returned by prepare_input_files()), which skips all preprocessing.
  • prepare_input_files() requires the optional packages listed under Installation for deconvolution and prior-network assembly.
  • The original Python implementation is available at https://github.com/SysBioOncology/RaCInG.
